scams.name: Pickpocketing
scams.description: Pickpockets operate in tourist-heavy areas and crowded public transport. They work in teams using distraction techniques - asking directions, bumping into you, or creating commotion while accomplices steal. At Confluence Tram stop, groups surround tourists to access backpacks. On Metro Line D and T2 tram, pickpockets target chaotic boarding/exiting moments.
scams.avoidance: Wear bags across your body with zippers facing inward. Keep minimal cash and one card on you. Use money belts or hidden pouches. Stay alert during metro boarding and exiting.
scams.location: Vieux Lyon, Place Bellecour, Part-Dieu station, Perrache station, Metro Line D, T2 tram

scams.name: Fake Metro Ticket Scam
scams.description: Ticket touts approach confused tourists at major stations offering metro tickets at 'reasonable' prices. The tickets are fake, expired, or already used. The scammer claims extra tickets or offers discounts compared to official machines. When you try to use the ticket, it won't work at the turnstile.
scams.avoidance: Only buy tickets from official TCL machines or counters. Use the TCL mobile app for digital tickets. Ignore anyone offering to sell tickets outside official channels.

scams.name: Fake Charity/Petition Scam
scams.description: Someone approaches with a clipboard asking 'Do you speak English?' requesting signatures for a deaf-mute charity. After signing, they flip to a donation section pressuring you for money. While distracted with the clipboard, an accomplice may pickpocket you from behind.
scams.avoidance: Say 'Non, merci' and keep walking. Never sign anything on the street. Legitimate French charities only ask for email, not cash. Keep one hand on belongings if stopped.
scams.location: Rue de la République, Part-Dieu station, Perrache station, Place Bellecour

scams.name: Restaurant Overcharging
scams.description: Tourist restaurants near historic areas present inflated bills: adding items not ordered, charging for 'free' bread/water, using elevated 'tourist menus,' or hiding details in French-only fine print. Some trade on Lyon's gastronomic reputation to justify excessive prices for mediocre food.
scams.avoidance: Check prices before sitting down. Ask for itemized bills and review carefully. Use Google Translate for French menus. Eat where locals eat. Confirm prices when ordering wine or specials.

scams.name: Shell Game / Three-Card Monte
scams.description: A scammer sets up with cups or cards inviting bets. 'Winners' in the crowd are accomplices. The game is completely rigged through sleight of hand - you cannot win. The operator may let you win small to build confidence, then take your money on larger bets.
scams.avoidance: Never play street gambling games - always rigged. Don't stop to watch. Remember bystanders are likely accomplices.
scams.location: Busy tourist areas, near major attractions, metro exits

scams.name: Gold Ring Scam
scams.description: Someone 'finds' a gold ring near you asking if you dropped it. When you say no, they claim it's real gold and offer to sell it for a 'good price.' The ring is worthless brass. They may also ask for money for food or family.
scams.avoidance: Don't engage - say 'Non' and keep walking. Never accept items 'found' on the street.
scams.location: Tourist walkways, near bridges, pedestrian areas

scams.name: Friendship Bracelet Scam
scams.description: A vendor grabs your hand and quickly weaves a bracelet around your wrist. Once tied with a difficult knot, they demand €10-20 payment. If you refuse, they become aggressive or an accomplice uses the distraction to pickpocket you.
scams.avoidance: Keep hands in pockets when approached. Say 'Non' firmly and keep walking. Don't let anyone touch you or attach anything.
scams.location: Tourist attractions, near churches, pedestrian areas

scams.name: Rose/Flower Scam
scams.description: A seller approaches couples dining outdoors offering a rose. The moment you touch or accept it, they demand €5-10. If you try to return it, they refuse and become aggressive until you pay out of embarrassment.
scams.avoidance: Don't touch or accept flowers offered. A simple 'Non, merci' sends them away. Ask restaurant staff to intervene if needed.
scams.location: Restaurant terraces, romantic spots, evening entertainment areas

scams.name: Fake Police Scam
scams.description: Criminals pose as police, quickly flashing fake badges. They claim to check your wallet for counterfeit bills or 'drug money.' While examining your wallet, they steal cash. Sometimes a 'tourist' accomplice first asks you to break a large bill, then the fake officer arrives.
scams.avoidance: Real police never ask to see your wallet - only ID documents. Ask to see badge clearly. Suggest going to nearest police station. Call 17 if unsure.
scams.location: Metro stations, tourist areas, near bars at night

scams.name: Taxi Overcharging
scams.description: Drivers may take long routes, 'forget' to start the meter, or select higher night/weekend rates during regular hours. Airport runs are vulnerable - Lyon-Saint Exupéry to city center should be €50-70. Unlicensed 'gypsy cabs' quote low then demand more upon arrival.
scams.avoidance: Only use taxis from official ranks. Ensure meter is zeroed before departure. Know approximate fares in advance. Use GPS to follow route. Consider Uber or Bolt.
scams.location: Lyon-Saint Exupéry Airport, Part-Dieu station, Perrache station, outside nightclubs

scams.name: ATM Skimming / Private ATM Scam
scams.description: Criminals attach skimming devices to ATMs stealing card data and PINs. Private ATMs like Euronet charge excessive fees and poor exchange rates - up to 4x more than bank ATMs. They offer Dynamic Currency Conversion at terrible rates.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside bank branches only. Look for major French banks: BNP Paribas, Société Générale, LCL. Cover keypad when entering PIN. Wiggle card slot before inserting. Decline dynamic currency conversion.
scams.location: Private ATMs in tourist areas, ATMs on busy streets, near train stations

scams.name: Broken Camera Scam
scams.description: Someone asks you to take their photo using their camera. After returning it, they claim you broke it and demand repair money. The camera was already broken - they use it repeatedly for this scam.
scams.avoidance: Politely decline to take photos with others' cameras. If accused of damage, suggest filing a police report together - scammers will refuse.
